prompt: What does this course do with a word like "partition" or "stream"?
hint: It is the map, not the territory.

choices.text: Names it, and shows it happening once
choices.why: Right: the vocabulary, seen once on your own machine.

choices.text: Teaches the tools that implement it, in full depth and with every option
choices.why: That is what the courses after it spend forty or seventy hours on.

choices.text: Leaves it for a later course in the track to define properly
choices.why: The later courses assume the word; this is where it is learnt.

choices.text: Defines it in a glossary at the end
choices.why: There is no glossary: each word is met where it happens.

prompt: Where does the data used in this course come from?

choices.text: From a public data set published by a real bicycle-sharing company
choices.why: Roda Livre does not exist, and nothing is downloaded.

choices.text: From short programs the lessons print, run from fixed seeds
choices.why: Right, which is why your numbers match the text.

choices.text: From files the platform copies to your machine
choices.why: The platform runs and copies nothing; you run everything.

choices.text: From the sample data inside pyarrow
choices.why: pyarrow is a library for formats, not a source of data.

prompt: A lesson reaches the point where writing SQL queries would be the next step. What does it do?

choices.text: Teaches enough SQL to finish the example
choices.why: That would be teaching another course’s subject badly.

choices.text: Skips the step without saying anything
choices.why: It says where the subject continues.

choices.text: Names `sql-databases`, and stops
choices.why: Right: each edge of the course names the course beyond it.

choices.text: Asks the student to look the syntax up online
choices.why: The course points at a course, not at a search.

prompt: Why could nobody at Roda Livre answer "which stations ran out last week" on Monday?
hint: Think about what each system was built for.

choices.text: It was spread over three systems
choices.why: Right: the data existed, but not in an answerable shape.

choices.text: The question needed a machine-learning model to be trained first
choices.why: It asks what happened, not what will happen.

choices.text: Nobody had recorded which docks held bicycles
choices.why: The sensors record that every minute; they just keep it two days.

choices.text: The app database was too slow to query
choices.why: Speed was not the obstacle; shape and history were.

prompt: The app database keeps the current state of every bicycle. Why is that a problem for Marta’s question?
hint: Her question is about last week.

choices.text: The current state is stored in a binary format that nobody can read
choices.why: It is readable; it is just not history.

choices.text: Last week’s state has been overwritten
choices.why: Right: a system built to charge customers keeps now, not then.

choices.text: The state is only updated once a month
choices.why: It is updated on every ride.

choices.text: Current state includes bicycles in broken docks
choices.why: True, but that is a definition problem, not a history problem.

prompt: Which of these is the data engineer’s part of answering Marta’s question?

choices.text: Deciding that "ran out" means zero bicycles available for five minutes or more
choices.why: That definition is the analyst’s.

choices.text: Predicting which stations will run out on Friday
choices.why: That is the data scientist’s next question.

choices.text: Putting the sensors, rides and repairs on one clock in one place
choices.why: Right: that is what makes the question answerable at all.

choices.text: Drawing the chart Marta will look at
choices.why: The chart is the analyst’s delivery.

prompt: The spreadsheet arrives with a column `doca` instead of `dock`. Which outcome does a well-built load produce?
hint: Compare a loud failure with a quiet one.

choices.text: It loads the file and marks every dock as unbroken
choices.why: That is the quiet failure: a plausible, wrong table.

choices.text: It stops and says which column it could not find
choices.why: Right: nobody downstream receives a wrong answer.

choices.text: It guesses that `doca` means `dock` and carries on
choices.why: A guess that is right today is wrong the day the guess is wrong.

choices.text: It skips the spreadsheet and loads the other two
choices.why: Silently missing data is still a wrong answer.

prompt: Why did one Wednesday have 27 hours of sensor readings?
hint: Curitiba is three hours behind UTC.

choices.text: The sensors sent each reading three times
choices.why: Duplicates would multiply readings, not add exactly three hours.

choices.text: Readings began arriving in UTC
choices.why: Right: three hours of one day were labelled as the next.

choices.text: Daylight saving time started that week
choices.why: It would move one hour, and Brazil no longer uses it.

choices.text: A dock was installed in another time zone
choices.why: All twelve stations are in Curitiba.

prompt: Match each role to what it delivers.
hint: Ask what each one hands to somebody else.

pairs.right: data that arrives on time and correct
agreed definitions of the business’s numbers

prompt: What is wrong with the picture of data roles as a ladder?
hint: Rungs are ranked; these are not.

choices.text: They are different jobs, not ranks
choices.why: Right: different deliveries, not seniority.

choices.text: The ladder is upside down: engineers are the most senior
choices.why: Turning the ladder over keeps the wrong idea of a ladder.

choices.text: There are really only two roles in the field, not five
choices.why: There are five names for five kinds of work.

choices.text: Analysts and scientists are the same job
choices.why: One explains what happened; the other predicts and tests.

prompt: Two dashboards show different totals for "active customers". Which role’s work is missing?

choices.text: The machine learning engineer’s
choices.why: No model is involved in a count.

choices.text: The data scientist’s
choices.why: Prediction is not the problem; agreement is.

choices.text: The analytics engineer’s, who keeps one agreed definition
choices.why: Right: one definition in one place.

choices.text: Nobody’s: dashboards always differ
choices.why: Two numbers for one thing is a defect, not a fact of life.

prompt: Caio’s model predicts demand well in his notebook but nothing in the app uses it. Whose work is that gap?
hint: Production is a different place from a notebook.

choices.text: The analyst’s
choices.why: Analysts answer questions; they do not deploy models.

choices.text: The data engineer’s, who feeds the model its data
choices.why: He feeds the data; running the model in the app is another job.

choices.text: The machine learning engineer’s
choices.why: Right: a model running in production, fed and monitored.

choices.text: The data scientist’s, by definition
choices.why: He proves it predicts; making it answer in the app is another job.

prompt: Which of these make the data engineer’s work different from an analyst’s? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It is software that runs every day
choices.why: Yes: a pipeline is never finished.

choices.text: Its users are mostly other systems and data people
choices.why: Yes: Marta sees only its absence.

choices.text: Its failures are quiet
choices.why: Yes: a double load looks fine.

choices.text: It needs no SQL
choices.why: It uses SQL every day.

prompt: A job advert asks one person for pipelines, dashboards, A/B tests and model deployment. What is it really asking for?
hint: Count the roles in the list.

choices.text: A senior data scientist
choices.why: Seniority does not merge four jobs into one.

choices.text: A small team
choices.why: Right: the roles name kinds of work, and this is four.

choices.text: An analytics engineer
choices.why: That role is the definitions, not deployment or tests.

choices.text: A database administrator
choices.why: None of those four is keeping one database fast.

prompt: Which question does the data engineer start from?

choices.text: What will happen, and why?
choices.why: That is the data scientist’s.

choices.text: What happened last month?
choices.why: That is the analyst’s.

choices.text: Which model should we deploy to the app this quarter?
choices.why: That is closer to the ML engineer.

choices.text: Will the data be there, and right?
choices.why: Right.

prompt: In Davi’s week, what were most of the items?
hint: Two requests, one design question, and the rest.

choices.text: New pipelines built from scratch
choices.why: Only the requests were new work.

choices.text: Things that broke
choices.why: Right: six of nine.

choices.text: Meetings about strategy and the platform’s future
choices.why: There were none in the list.

choices.text: Training models for Caio
choices.why: Caio trains his own models.

prompt: Match each event of the week to the kind of work it is.

pairs.left: a ride appeared twice after a retry
the API refused calls past 100 a minute

prompt: What does "a pipeline is built to be operated" ask of it?
hint: Think of the person on call at 06:00.

choices.text: That it runs as fast as possible
choices.why: Speed is not on the list.

choices.text: That it uses one language
choices.why: Language is irrelevant to operating it.

choices.text: That it reports failures and is safe to rerun
choices.why: Right: those three make it operable.

choices.text: That only its author changes it
choices.why: The opposite: somebody else must be able to tell what it did.

prompt: Put the levels of Monica Rogati’s pyramid in order, from the bottom.
hint: Each level rests on the one beneath.
trap: Learning comes last because it needs everything below it.

prompt: A company hires a data scientist before anyone has built the bottom of the pyramid. What happens, according to the section?

choices.text: Models on raw data work fine
choices.why: There is no reliable data to build on.

choices.text: The scientist spends the first year doing data engineering
choices.why: Right, usually without the tools for it.

choices.text: The company skips straight to optimisation
choices.why: The top cannot stand without the bottom.

choices.text: Nothing changes; the levels are independent
choices.why: Each level rests on the ones beneath it.

prompt: How is a data engineer different from a database administrator?

choices.text: One tends a single system; the other moves data between many
choices.why: Right: the engineer owns what happens in between.

choices.text: The administrator writes no SQL at all, only configuration
choices.why: Administrators write a great deal of it.

choices.text: The engineer never touches a database
choices.why: He reads from them every day.

choices.text: They are two names for one job
choices.why: The job borrows from administration; it is not it.

prompt: Put the three eras in the order they began.
trap: ELT only made sense once storing raw data became cheap.

prompt: In ETL, the T stands for ___.
Why did "data engineer" become a common title in the big-data era?
hint: What did processing data turn into?

choices.text: Because warehouses were invented then
choices.why: Warehouses are from the 1990s.

choices.text: Because the work became writing programs
choices.why: Right: the work had become software engineering.

choices.text: Because the cloud made ETL unnecessary
choices.why: The cloud came later, and moved the T rather than removing it.

choices.text: Because relational databases stopped being used by web companies
choices.why: They are still the commonest source of all.

prompt: What made ELT cheaper than ETL in the cloud era?
hint: Where does the transformation run in ELT?

choices.text: Cheap storage and warehouses that scale
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Transformations became unnecessary
choices.why: They still happen; they happen later.

choices.text: Sources started sending clean, ready-to-use data to the warehouse
choices.why: They did not, and they still do not.

choices.text: Loading became slower than transforming
choices.why: Speed of loading is not the reason given.

prompt: Which questions have stayed the same across all three eras? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Did all of it arrive?
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Did any of it arrive twice?
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Which vendor is cheapest this year?
choices.why: That changes with the tools; it is not one of the four.

choices.text: Is it here in time?
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Installed, because a virtual environment is just a directory

choices.why: A virtual environment needs none.

prompt: Why are the library versions pinned with `==`?

prompt: `python3 -m venv .venv` says "ensurepip is not available". What is missing?

prompt: A new terminal answers `import pyarrow` with `ModuleNotFoundError`, an hour after it worked. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: pyarrow uninstalled itself
choices.why: Packages do not leave on their own.

choices.text: The environment is not active
choices.why: Right: the system’s Python has never heard of pyarrow.

choices.text: The disk filled up while the terminal was open
choices.why: A full disk fails when writing, not on import.

choices.text: The version pin was wrong
choices.why: It installed and worked an hour ago.

prompt: On Ubuntu 22.04, `pip install pyarrow==26.0.0` answers "No matching distribution found". What does that tell you?

choices.text: The version was mistyped
choices.why: 26.0.0 exists; the transcript lists it.

choices.text: pip needs upgrading
choices.why: An old pip is not the reason here.

choices.text: PyPI is down
choices.why: Then it could not list any versions at all.

choices.text: The Python is 3.10, older than pyarrow 26 needs
choices.why: Right: it needs 3.11 or newer.

prompt: An error you do not recognise fills the screen. Where do you start reading?

choices.text: At the first error it printed

choices.text: At the line with the most words

choices.text: At the middle of the output

choices.text: Nowhere: reinstall the operating system

choices.text: Nobody gets a wrong number

choices.text: A dashboard of today’s readings
